criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly identifies genuine cross-cutting AI-platform concerns (provider-abstraction gateway, resilience via retries/backoff/failover, observability with token+cost attribution and trace propagation, versioned prompt registry, shared eval harness, guardrails/secrets) and places each correctly relative to product code; interface and evolution claims are sound (semver, backward-compat contract, deprecation window, provider-native passthrough); reliability claims (SPOF/HA, circuit breakers, per-tenant quotas/bulkheads, proxy latency, caching) are accurate. Deduct for invented mechanisms, mislabeled responsibilities, or a design that would break clients or leak provider features.

Full marks require all four requested dimensions: (1) the reusable component set with ownership, (2) the explicit platform/product boundary, (3) the standards & governance including a versioning/backward-compat/deprecation story and observability/cost conventions, and (4) the centralization-vs-autonomy trade-off with failure modes and mitigations. Also requires an adoption strategy and at least one escape-hatch/extension mechanism. Partial credit scales with dimensions meaningfully covered.

Full marks: justifies why each concern belongs in the shared layer versus the product (undifferentiated/reliability-security-cost vs product behavior), frames adoption as a DX/paved-road problem rather than a mandate, and weighs the centralization trade-off by tying concrete consequences (bottleneck, SPOF, noisy neighbors, leaky abstraction) to specific mitigations instead of asserting one correct design. Deduct for unsupported assertions or ignoring the tension between central control and team autonomy.

Full marks: cleanly separates components, boundary, standards, and trade-offs; uses platform-engineering vocabulary precisely (golden path/paved road, inner-source, contract testing, canary, feature flags, bulkhead, deprecation window, SLA); reads as a senior design-review proposal. Deduct for disorganized structure, vague hand-waving, or misused terminology.

expected_answer_points: Enumerates concrete reusable components with clear ownership: an LLM gateway (provider abstraction, key/auth management, rate limiting, retries/backoff, failover, caching), a thin client SDK, an observability + per-request token/cost-accounting layer, a versioned prompt registry, a shared eval/regression harness, and guardrails/secrets management

Draws an explicit platform-vs-product boundary with a decision rule: platform owns undifferentiated cross-cutting concerns (resilience, provider abstraction, security, observability, cost); teams own prompt content, orchestration/business logic, UX, and their own eval data

Specifies interface and versioning standards: a stable, versioned (semver) provider-agnostic API with a backward-compatibility contract, a deprecation policy (migration window, contract tests), the ability to add providers/models without breaking clients, and safe rollout via canary/feature flags

Defines cross-system observability and cost-attribution conventions to mandate (trace-context propagation, cost tags per team/feature/model, structured logging with PII redaction) — mandating conventions rather than implementations

Treats adoption as a developer-experience / paved-road problem rather than a mandate: the golden path is the easiest path, with documented escape hatches/passthrough and inner-source contribution to prevent the central team becoming a bottleneck

Addresses the gateway as a single point of failure and noisy-neighbor risk: HA/failover, circuit breakers, client fallback to direct provider calls, per-tenant quotas/bulkheads, and a proxy latency/caching budget
Avoids a leaky lowest-common-denominator abstraction by passing through provider-native features (streaming, tool/function calling, structured outputs) and fast-following new capabilities
Analyzes the centralization-vs-autonomy trade-off explicitly, pairing each concrete failure mode with a mitigation rather than asserting a single 'right' design
common_pitfalls: Answers by naming a vendor or library (e.g., 'just deploy LiteLLM / an API gateway') without defining component boundaries, ownership, or the engineering standards that make it adopted
Over-centralizes: routes all traffic through a rigid gateway with no escape hatches or extension points, ignoring team autonomy — which in practice drives shadow/bypass implementations
Ignores the gateway as a single point of failure and the noisy-neighbor problem (no HA, no client fallback, no per-tenant quotas), turning the platform into a reliability liability
Designs a lowest-common-denominator API that hides provider-native features (streaming, tool/function calling, structured outputs) — the classic leaky abstraction that pushes teams off the platform

Blurs the boundary by putting product-specific concerns (business prompt content, domain orchestration) into the shared layer, or pushing cross-cutting concerns like key management down into each team
Treats adoption as a compliance mandate and omits any versioning, backward-compatibility, or deprecation policy, so the platform silently breaks downstream teams and loses their trust
reference_answer:
**Reusable components (the shared platform).** (1) LLM gateway/proxy — one provider-agnostic endpoint that normalizes request/response across OpenAI, Anthropic and self-hosted models and centralizes auth/key management, rate limiting, retries with exponential backoff + jitter, timeouts, provider failover/routing, and response caching. It passes provider-native features (streaming, tool/function calling, structured outputs) through rather than hiding them. (2) A thin client SDK — the golden-path library teams import; it propagates trace context, gives typed requests and sane defaults, and holds no business logic. (3) Observability + cost layer — structured logging of prompt/response with PII redaction, distributed tracing, and per-request token/cost accounting tagged by team/feature/model, with budgets and alerts. (4) A versioned prompt registry — prompts/templates as reviewable artifacts (semver or content hash) with history and rollback, decoupled from code deploys. (5) A shared eval/regression harness — golden datasets and CI gates so every team measures quality and regressions the same way. (6) Guardrails and a secrets vault — centralized moderation/PII handling so keys never sprawl into repos.

**Boundary.** The platform owns undifferentiated, cross-cutting concerns: provider abstraction, resilience, security/compliance, observability, and cost governance. Product teams own the differentiated work: actual prompt content, orchestration/agent logic, business rules, UX, and their own eval datasets. Rule of thumb — if it's the same for everyone and getting it wrong is a reliability, security, or cost problem, it's platform; if it encodes product behavior, it's the team's.

**Standards & governance.** Treat the gateway as an internal product with an SLA. Ship a stable, versioned (semver) provider-agnostic API with a written backward-compatibility contract and a deprecation policy: announce, dual-run, migration window, and contract tests that fail CI when a change breaks a client. New providers/models onboard behind the same interface without breaking callers; roll changes out via canary + feature flags. Mandate conventions, not implementations — trace-id propagation, cost tags, structured logs. Make the golden path the easiest path (better DX than rolling your own) with documented escape hatches (raw passthrough), and inner-source the platform so teams contribute instead of forking.

**Centralization vs autonomy.** Bottleneck: a central team gatekeeping every change stalls teams — mitigate with self-service, inner-source contributions, and middleware/extension points. SPOF: all traffic flows through the gateway — mitigate with HA/multi-region, circuit breakers, a client fallback to direct provider calls on outage, a tight proxy latency budget, and caching. Noisy neighbors: one team's spike starves others — mitigate with per-tenant quotas and bulkhead isolation. Leaky abstraction: a lowest-common-denominator API that hides streaming/tool-use drives teams to bypass it — mitigate with native passthrough and fast-follow on new capabilities. Adoption is won by DX and trust, not mandate: if bypassing is easier than compliance, the platform fails.
